Great paper from Amazon and colleagues on self-improving multi-agent systems.

Episodic memory for agents is so underrated.

But I am starting to see lots of good applications as frontier models improve.

This paper is the latest example.

They built a system that has three parts, all run by the same LLM. A controller plans each task and runs it one step at a time, choosing which sub-agent and which skills to use at each step. Sub-agents start as a generalist, and each specialist inherits the generalist's prompt plus its own role-specific method. Skills are short procedures, such as algorithms or pitfall checklists.

EMMA treats the controller's routing memory, the agent prompts, and the skills as episodic memory that improves from failures. After a failed task, a reflector decides which of the three owns the fix and proposes one edit there. Guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental, and bounded.

EMMA beats ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS, and ADAS on KramaBench, AppWorld, and BBEH, by up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, and uses 17 to 38% fewer training executions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35966

Tests check examples. Proofs check everything.

Anthropic and Theorem used Claude to formally verify security properties in 123 open-source libraries at the RISC-V assembly level, in a few weeks. For every input under 64 MB, the proven programs exit normally, with no memory-safety errors or failed assertions, under stated assumptions. Along the way Claude found bugs that had survived trillions of test runs.

For scale: the seL4 kernel took two person-years to build and twenty to formally verify. That cost kept proofs inside avionics and kernels until now.

the default that costs you: reading a green test suite as proof. A test checks the inputs someone thought of, and the bug sits in the one nobody tried.

the version you can run today: before asking a model for tests, ask it for properties.

"List the properties this function must hold for every input: what it never returns, when it must never crash, and what two implementations must always agree on. Then write property-based tests that throw thousands of random inputs at each one."

the check: break the function on purpose. A useful property fails on the broken version. If nothing fails, the property is too weak.

For the agreement step I use a prompt that compares two implementations with property-based testing. It is the testing cousin of what Anthropic did when it proved behavioral equivalence for a Python interpreter written in Rust.

Theorem is publishing a Claude skill for developers who want to verify their own code.

the property-based comparison prompt:

https://godofprompt.ai/prompt-library/compare-function-outputs

text:
You use Claude to write emails. One guy used it to run 11 labs, and Anthropic just bought his company.

That gap is the whole skill now: using Claude as your operations team, not your writer.

His name is Cody Tranbarger. No employees. Just him, part-time consultants and, in his words, "a bunch of Claude." With Claude he coordinated 11 outside labs. In under 18 months his treatment for a rare form of muscular dystrophy went from idea to promising results in mice.

Anthropic announced the acquisition of his company, Mithril Medicine, yesterday. Cody now works there.

My take: the labs did the science. Keeping 11 vendors, contracts and deadlines moving is a job that usually takes a whole team. He did it with Claude. You can run any project with 5+ moving parts the same way:

“Here are my vendors and what each owes me. Build a tracker with deliverable, deadline, status and next action. Flag anything due in 7 days or waiting on me.”
“Write a follow-up to [vendor] under 80 words. Restate the deadline and what I need, and end with one yes-or-no question.”
“Read this contract. Pull out payment terms, deadlines, IP ownership and cancellation terms. Flag what a small business should push back on.”
“Using my tracker, plan my week by what unblocks the most work.”

What would you run solo if Claude handled the coordination?
Source, Anthropic's write-up on Mithril: https://www.anthropic.com/research/early-progress-drug-development
